papers.title: Numerical analysis of coupled flow, deformation and frictional contact mechanics in a fractured porous medium
authors: Marius Nevland, Kundan Kumar, Inga Berre, Jakub Wiktor Both, Eirik Keilegavlen
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.14341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper studies the numerical approximation of a mathematical model of coupled flow and viscoelastic deformation in a fractured porous medium including fracture contact mechanics. We consider a mixed-dimensional model, where the fracture is modeled as a co-dimension one object within the porous medium. This model couples Darcy flow in the matrix and fracture, linear viscoelasticity of the matrix and frictional contact mechanics of the fracture surfaces; the contact conditions include normal compliance and a Coulomb friction law. We propose and analyze a fully discrete numerical scheme for this problem, using conformal finite elements in space and the implicit Euler method in time. papers.title: MC$^2$: Monte Carlo Correction for Fast Elliptic PDE Solving
authors: Ethan Hsu, Hong Meng Yam, Ivan Ge
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2605.09288v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Partial differential equation (PDE) solvers underpin modern computer graphics, geometry processing, and scientific computing. Classical Monte Carlo PDE solvers such as Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) provide mesh-free estimations that are unbiased, but with accuracy limited by sampling and numerical approximation. Learned solvers are fast but biased and brittle under distribution shift. We therefore present MC$^2$, a hybrid Neural Network-Monte Carlo PDE solver that treats a low-budget Monte Carlo solution as a structured estimator of the true field and learns a single-pass neural correction to recover a high-fidelity solution. papers.title: FP64 Performance and the Limits of Ozaki Emulation on HPC Systems
authors: Katarzyna (Kasia),  Swirydowicz, Nicholas Malaya, Noah Wolfe, Paul Bauman, Pieter Ghysels, Jonathan Belof
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2611.13332v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A growing industry narrative holds that native double precision can be deprioritized in HPC accelerators, on the hypothesis that low-precision tensor cores can emulate FP64 on demand, and that most HPC workloads are bandwidth-bound. This paper evaluates some of those claims and explores the importance of FP64 in scientific computing. We show roofline profiling data of representative HPC workloads, across a variety of common computational motifs, to evaluate the arithmetic-intensity and accuracy requirements of these workloads. We also consider FP64 emulation via the Ozaki method to ascertain some of the possibilities and limitations of these approaches.
